title: The Boy Jesus at the Temple
note:
Built from the curriculum photographs in Drive’s Beginner → Chapter 18 → “01 - Curriculum Source”: three pages, p.83 (title, prayer, Bible portion), p.84 (the lesson and “Tell the Answers”) and p.86 (My Decision, the song line, the Memory Verse and the Concluding Prayer).

**p.85 is not in Drive.** The folder was paginated to the end and holds exactly three photographs, and the page numbers jump from 84 to 86 — the same shape as Chapter 14, which skipped p.65. By the shape of this book the missing page is the activity page. Nothing here depends on it: all six printed questions are on p.84 and every answer is in the lesson above them. Worth a photograph if it carries something.

**Both of this chapter’s prayers are not where you would expect.** p.83’s opening prayer is printed in full; p.86’s Concluding Prayer is the stage direction “(Let one child pray. )”. So `prayer` carries the **opening** prayer, as in Chapter 15 and unlike Chapters 12, 14 and 17 where it was the other way round. And there is no `song`: p.86’s “Learn to sing” says only “(Sing a suitable English song.)”, which is an instruction to the teacher, exactly as in Chapter 17.

**A small mismatch between a question and the lesson, flagged rather than patched.** Printed question 4 asks “How long did Jesus sit in the Temple among the teachers.?”. p.84 says only “After three days they found him in the temple courts” — which is how long the *searching* took, not how long he sat. The answer the book is looking for is three days and that is what the second game teaches, but it asks the question the lesson can actually answer: how long until they found him. An editorial question for the teacher.

The stray full stops before the question marks — “year.?”, “journey.?”, “festival.?”, “teachers.?”, “this.?” — are the book’s and are carried verbatim in `curriculum`. The same stop appears inside the Memory Verse on p.86.

**Artwork.** Thirteen panels and both covers came from Drive’s “04 - Story Artwork”, all fifteen distinct by SHA-256, the folder enumerated by exact filename rather than by paging. The twenty-seven text cards this chapter first shipped with are gone rather than reconciled, which is what happened to Beginner Chapters 5 to 17 and to Primary 1 to 3. Each card is now a picture with `alt` describing the scene and quoting what is lettered on it.

This is the kindest set of panels the class has had for shelf cards: twelve of the thirteen survive the square centre crop with their lettering whole, where Chapter 17 managed three of ten. Only panel 2 is cut. Two panels are barred on content instead — 10 and 11 letter the answers to printed questions 5 and 6 — and all four games still have a picture.

Panels 4 and 5 are 941×1671, one pixel short of the canonical 941×1672. Converted without distortion and nothing resized them.

**Three things in the artwork worth the teacher’s eye.**

1. **Panels 6 and 7 carry the same caption, word for word** — “After travelling for a day, Mary and Joseph realized that Jesus was not with them. They began looking for Him among their relatives and friends.” The scenes differ, the road and then the camp, and both are good; the repetition reads as a duplicated caption rather than a deliberate beat. Carried as drawn and recorded here.

2. **Panel 12 softens the lesson’s last line.** p.84 ends “But they did not understand what he was saying to them”; the panel reads “When they heard this, they did not say anything.” Not understanding and not speaking are different things, and the lesson’s is the harder and more interesting one. The `celebration` and the story still follow the lesson.

3. **Panel 11 letters the Memory Verse exactly** — “Didn’t you know I had to be in my Father’s house?”, with “my Father’s house” picked out in colour. It is the only confirmation of the wording outside p.86, and it agrees with what the verse carries, including the plain question mark where p.86 prints “.?”.

cover.note: Both drawn and imported, both at the canonical sizes — 941×1672 portrait and 1672×941 landscape.

story.alt: A boy with a backpack stands at the open door of a church, pointing up at the cross on the gable, families going in ahead of him and Halo glowing beside him. The caption reads, “Have you ever wondered why we go to church? It is a special place where we come together to worship God, learn about Him, and grow together.” Halo asks, “Where do we go to worship God?” and the boy answers, “To church!”

Inside the church, stained glass and a wooden cross, a band playing and a woman reading from a Bible at the front, children in the pews with their hands folded. The caption reads, “At church, we come together to worship God, learn His Word, and grow together.” Halo says, “That’s right! Look at all the ways we can be part of God’s house!”, a girl says, “We can pray, sing, listen and learn!”, and Halo asks, “Exactly! And do you know who loved being in God’s house too?”

A golden ribbon of light opens out of the church and a sunlit city appears behind it, with a man, a woman and a boy walking in it. The caption reads, “Jesus loved going to God’s house too. When Jesus was twelve years old, something special happened in Jerusalem.” The boy asks, “Jesus?”, Halo answers, “Yes! Jesus.” and then, “Let’s go back in time and see what happened.”

Mary, Joseph and the boy Jesus walk together through a crowd toward the great gold-fronted temple, banners flying and pilgrims all around them. The caption reads, “Jesus and His family arrived in Jerusalem for the Festival of the Passover. They travelled together with their relatives and friends and spent the festival in Jerusalem.”

A long column of travellers winds away down a hillside road with the city on the ridge behind them, Mary and Joseph among them. The caption reads, “After the festival was over, Mary and Joseph began the journey home with their relatives and friends. They thought Jesus was travelling with the group.”

Mary has stopped on the road with a hand on Joseph’s arm, both of them looking back. The caption reads, “After travelling for a day, Mary and Joseph realized that Jesus was not with them. They began looking for Him among their relatives and friends.” Mary asks, “Where is Jesus?” and Joseph answers, “Let’s look for Him among our relatives and friends.”

The camp at the roadside, tents and loaded donkeys and barrels, Mary turning among the crowd with her hand at her chest while Joseph shades his eyes and searches. The caption is the same as the panel before it, word for word: “After travelling for a day, Mary and Joseph realized that Jesus was not with them. They began looking for Him among their relatives and friends.”

Mary and Joseph walking back up the road toward Jerusalem, the walled city ahead of them, other travellers passing the other way. The caption reads, “They could not find Jesus among their relatives and friends. So they went back to Jerusalem to look for Him.” Mary says, “We must go back to Jerusalem.” and Joseph answers, “Yes. We will find Him.”

The boy Jesus sits on the temple steps among bearded teachers, one hand raised as he speaks, the men leaning in to listen, and Mary and Joseph coming up the steps behind them. The caption reads, “After three days, they found Him in the Temple courts, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking questions.”

Mary kneels down to Jesus on the steps with a hand on his shoulder, Joseph behind her. The caption reads, “When His parents saw Him, they were amazed. Mary spoke to Jesus.” Mary says, “Son, why have you treated us like this?” and “Your father and I have been anxiously searching for you.”

Jesus sits facing his mother with both hands open as he answers her, the teachers still around them. The caption reads, “Jesus answered His mother.” Jesus asks, “Why were you searching for me?” and “Didn’t you know I had to be in my Father’s house?”
Mary and Jesus sit together on the step, looking at each other, Joseph standing quietly behind with his hand to his chin. The caption reads, “When they heard this, they did not say anything.”

Back in the present, the boy sits in a church pew with a Bible on his lap looking up at Halo, a priest preaching at the lectern and other children in the pews around him. The caption reads, “Jesus loved being in His Father’s house and learning about God. We can also take part in God’s house.” Halo says, “Just like Jesus, we can learn, worship, and take part in church.” and the boy answers, “I can be part of God’s house too!”

curriculum.source: Beginners Mar Thoma Vol-1, Chapter 18 “The Boy Jesus at the Temple”, p.84 — “Tell the Answers”
curriculum.note: All six questions transcribed from the printed page, punctuation included — the stray full stops before the question marks are the book’s, not typos here. Questions 5 and 6 are a matched pair and the fourth game answers them together.

questions.question: Where did Jesus’ parents go every year.?
questions.objective: Remember that Jesus’ parents went to Jerusalem every year.
questions.answer: To Jerusalem. “Every year Jesus’ parents went to Jerusalem for the Festival of the Passover.” (p.84)

questions.question: What was the purpose of their journey.?
questions.objective: Remember that they went for the Festival of the Passover.
questions.answer: For the Festival of the Passover. Same sentence, p.84.

questions.question: At what age was Jesus taken to the festival.?
questions.objective: Remember that Jesus was twelve years old.
questions.answer: Twelve. “When he was twelve years old, they went up to the festival, according to the custom.” (p.84)

questions.question: How long did Jesus sit in the Temple among the teachers.?
questions.objective: Remember that it was three days before they found him.
questions.answer: Three days. “After three days they found him in the temple courts, sitting among the teachers…” (p.84) — the lesson gives the three days as the length of the search; see the chapter note.

questions.question: “Why have you treated us like this.?” Who said to whom?
questions.objective: Remember that his mother said it to Jesus.
questions.answer: His mother said it to Jesus. “His mother said to him, ‘Son, why have you treated us like this?’” (p.84)

questions.question: “Why were you searching for me?”. Who said to whom?
questions.objective: Remember that Jesus said it to his mother.
questions.answer: Jesus said it to his mother. “‘Why were you searching for me?’ he asked.” (p.84)

games.title: Every Year to Jerusalem
games.objective: Remember where Jesus' parents went each year, why they went, and how old Jesus was that year.

interactions.prompt: Match each one to the story.

games.note:
Three of the six printed questions in one board, because they are the three the lesson answers in its opening two sentences. “Every year → How often they went” is the fourth pair and is not padding: without it the board has three answers and three slots, so the last pair falls out by elimination rather than by being remembered.

Shelf picture panel-04. The family walking through the crowd toward the temple. The caption — which names Jerusalem and the Passover in its first line, two of this board’s three answers — is cropped away, so the card carries no lettering. What is left is the arrival itself, which a six-year-old cannot read a place-name or a festival off.

games.title: Three Days Looking
games.objective: Remember that it was three days before his parents found Jesus in the temple.

interactions.prompt: How long until they found him?

games.note:
Both wrong options are numbers the lesson actually uses — the one day they travelled before missing him, and the twelve years he was old — rather than other plausible numbers of days. A child who is guessing is choosing between three numbers that are all really in this story.

The printed question asks how long Jesus *sat* in the temple; p.84 says only that “after three days they found him in the temple courts”, which is how long the searching took. The game asks the question the lesson can actually answer — how long until they found him — and its answer is the book’s answer. The chapter note records the difference.

Shelf picture panel-08. Mary and Joseph walking back up the road to Jerusalem, still looking. Both bubbles survive the crop whole — “We must go back to Jerusalem.” and “Yes. We will find Him.” — and neither carries a number. It is the right card for a game about how long the search took because it is the search still going on. Panel 9 is the finding and panel 10 is the moment after it; both were left for later games or left out.

games.title: Looking for Him
games.objective: Follow what his parents did when they found Jesus was not with them.
games.note:
The one game that answers no printed question, kept because sequencing is the third skill the Beginner band asks for and because the middle of this story is a sequence: the festival ends, he stays, they travel a day, they search their relatives, they turn back. It stops at “They went back to Jerusalem” and never reaches the finding, so the three days the game before it asks for are not on the board.

Shelf picture panel-07. The roadside camp with Mary turning among the crowd and Joseph searching. No lettering survives the crop. It is one of the five steps this game asks a child to put in order, which is safe in a way a multiple choice would not be: a picture cannot encode a sequence, and all five steps are already on the board. Panel 6 was passed over because its bubble letters step four word for word.

games.title: Who Said It?
games.objective: Remember who spoke each of the two questions in the temple, and to whom.

interactions.prompt: Who said “Why have you treated us like this?”
interactions.hint: She had been searching for him.

interactions.prompt: Who said “Why were you searching for me?”
interactions.hint: He was the one they found.

games.note:
The two printed “who said to whom” questions, one after the other, with deliberately mirrored options: the right answer to the first is the first wrong answer to the second. A child cannot pattern-match their way through — they have to hold on to which of the two spoke which question, which is the whole of what questions 5 and 6 are asking.

Shelf picture panel-12. Mary and Jesus on the step afterwards, looking at each other, with Joseph behind. No lettering survives the crop, and that is the point: this game asks which of the two spoke which line, and the card shows both of them and says nothing. Panels 10 and 11 are the exchange itself and are barred from the whole shelf — 10 letters question 5’s answer and 11 letters question 6’s, and all four cards are read before any game is played.

verse.text: Didn’t you know I had to be in my Father’s house?

practice.hint: It begins by asking a question.
practice.note: Stage 1, recognition. The wrong options are ordinary phrases rather than invented scripture, and they are near-misses on the verb so that the child has to hear the actual word rather than the shape of the line.
Stage 2, phrase ordering. Three chunks, broken where the sense breathes. The build checks that they spell the verse exactly.

Stage 3, the missing word. Generated by the Memory Verse agent’s Beginner ladder and used as it came out, with one edit: the agent’s third option was “house?”, the verse’s closing question mark riding on the last token. A button that reads “house?” is a visible defect, so the mark was dropped. Beginner Chapter 12 had the same thing happen with a closing quote mark on “water” and Chapter 15 with an exclamation mark on “unity”; all three were fixed the same way. Prompt, hint and the other two options are untouched.

Stage 4, full reconstruction — five pieces where stage 2 had three, which is the whole of the difference between the two stages. Phrase chunks rather than single words, as every chapter in this class ships except Chapter 17, whose verse was five words long. The build checks that these five spell the verse exactly.

practice.prompt: Where does our verse come from?
practice.hint: The same book the lesson comes from.
practice.note:
Stage 5, the reference — recognised, not typed. Both distractors are verses this child has just learned: Psalm 119 was Chapter 17’s and Genesis 15 was Chapter 16’s.

St. Luke 2 is the **second** time this class has memorised from this chapter — Chapter 1’s verse was St Luke 2:30,31, Simeon in the same temple. A child who has kept that one already knows where this one lives, which is the kind of thing stage 5 is for.

verse.note:
Read from p.86 through the Memory Verse agent: `--fetch --source-dir` over the three curriculum photographs, the supervised read, then `--from-extraction`.

**Two things about how p.86 prints this verse.** It reads, in full: `He asked “Didn’t you know I had to be in my Father’s house.?”` The words “He asked” sit *outside* the quotation marks — they are the book’s narrative lead-in, not part of the verse — so the verse carried here is what is inside them. And the quotation closes with `.?`, a full stop and a question mark together, which is the same stray stop the book puts before the question mark in all six of this chapter’s printed questions; it is carried as a single `?`. Neither is a judgement about the wording, which is unchanged.

Five stages in the shape Chapters 1 to 9 and 11 to 17 of this class use — recognise, order, fill, rebuild, place. Stage 3 is the agent’s own Beginner rung with one option mark removed, explained there.

Translation is unresolved, which is where every other chapter in this class stands.

No second opinion — the teacher’s editorial Sheet was not available for this run.

decision.statement: I shall regularly go to Church and study the scriptures.
decision.note: The curriculum’s own My Decision from p.86, word for word.

prayer.text: Thank you Lord for the Church you have given us for worshipping you. Help us to utilize it for scripture studies, worship and community prayers. Amen.
prayer.note: The **opening** prayer from p.83, word for word. It is the opening one because p.86’s Concluding Prayer is the stage direction “(Let one child pray. )” rather than a prayer — the reverse of Chapters 12, 14 and 17, and the same as Chapter 15.

celebration.message: They found him in the temple, in his Father’s house.
celebration.note: The turn of the chapter, from p.84. Three days of searching end not in a telling-off that lands but in a boy saying, reasonably, that of course he was here.
